verses.text: Then we turned, and went up the way to Bashan. Og the king of Bashan came out against us, he and all his people, to battle at Edrei.
Yahweh said to me, “Don’t fear him; for I have delivered him, with all his people, and his land, into your hand. You shall do to him as you did to Sihon king of the Amorites, who lived at Heshbon.”
So Yahweh our God delivered into our hand Og also, the king of Bashan, and all his people. We struck him until no one was left to him remaining.
We took all his cities at that time. There was not a city which we didn’t take from them; sixty cities, all the region of Argob, the kingdom of Og in Bashan.
All these were cities fortified with high walls, gates, and bars; besides a great many villages without walls.
We utterly destroyed them, as we did to Sihon king of Heshbon, utterly destroying every inhabited city, with the women and the little ones.
But all the livestock, and the plunder of the cities, we took for plunder for ourselves.
We took the land at that time out of the hand of the two kings of the Amorites who were beyond the Jordan, from the valley of the Arnon to Mount Hermon.
(The Sidonians call Hermon Sirion, and the Amorites call it Senir.)
We took all the cities of the plain, and all Gilead, and all Bashan, to Salecah and Edrei, cities of the kingdom of Og in Bashan.

(For only Og king of Bashan remained of the remnant of the Rephaim. Behold, his bedstead was a bedstead of iron. Isn’t it in Rabbah of the children of Ammon? Nine cubits  was its length, and four cubits its width, after the cubit of a man.)
This land we took in possession at that time: from Aroer, which is by the valley of the Arnon, and half the hill country of Gilead, and its cities, gave I to the Reubenites and to the Gadites:
and the rest of Gilead, and all Bashan, the kingdom of Og, gave I to the half-tribe of Manasseh; all the region of Argob, even all Bashan. (The same is called the land of Rephaim.
Jair the son of Manasseh took all the region of Argob, to the border of the Geshurites and the Maacathites, and called them, even Bashan, after his own name, Havvoth Jair, to this day.)
I gave Gilead to Machir.

To the Reubenites and to the Gadites I gave from Gilead even to the valley of the Arnon, the middle of the valley, and its border, even to the river Jabbok, which is the border of the children of Ammon;
the Arabah also, and the Jordan and its border, from Chinnereth even to the sea of the Arabah, the Salt Sea, under the slopes of Pisgah eastward.
I commanded you at that time, saying, “Yahweh your God has given you this land to possess it. You shall pass over armed before your brothers the children of Israel, all the men of valor.
But your wives, and your little ones, and your livestock, (I know that you have much livestock), shall live in your cities which I have given you,

until Yahweh gives rest to your brothers, as to you, and they also possess the land which Yahweh your God gives them beyond the Jordan. Then you shall each return to his own possession, which I have given you.”
I commanded Joshua at that time, saying, “Your eyes have seen all that Yahweh your God has done to these two kings. So shall Yahweh do to all the kingdoms where you go over.
You shall not fear them; for Yahweh your God himself fights for you.”
I begged Yahweh at that time, saying,
“Lord  Yahweh, you have begun to show your servant your greatness, and your strong hand. For what god is there in heaven or in earth that can do works like yours, and mighty acts like yours?
Please let me go over and see the good land that is beyond the Jordan, that fine mountain, and Lebanon.”
But Yahweh was angry with me for your sakes, and didn’t listen to me. Yahweh said to me, “Let this satisfy you. Speak no more to me of this matter.
Go up to the top of Pisgah, and lift up your eyes westward, and northward, and southward, and eastward, and see with your eyes; for you shall not go over this Jordan.
But commission Joshua, and encourage him, and strengthen him; for he shall go over before this people, and he shall cause them to inherit the land which you shall see.”
So we stayed in the valley near Beth Peor.

footnotes.content: Og of Bashan — a giant king with a giant army — stood against them. Can you feel the weight of it? The turn toward Bashan meant facing one more obstacle before the promise. Sometimes the hardest battles come just before the threshold.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Before the sword swung once, the Lord had already placed the outcome in their hand. He speaks to Moses' fear first—'Don't fear him.' This is how mercy works: the victory is already won before we feel brave enough to step forward.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The text is plain: they struck until no one remained. This is the mercy of the conquest—final, absolute, with no lingering threat. Sometimes love means bringing something to an end so that new life can begin.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Sixty cities, all of them taken. Argob—the name means a place of stone heaps, a land of rolling highlands. The Lord's hand covers not just a king but a whole territory, a whole people's future inheritance. He gives abundantly.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: These cities were fortified—high walls, gates, bars—built to resist. Yet they fell. The world's strength crumbles before the Lord's purpose. What walls we build to protect ourselves often crumble too, when we finally learn to trust.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The language is stark: utter destruction. In the new creation, we won't need to interpret this as we read it now—we'll understand the holiness that required it. For now, we trust that the Judge of all the earth did right.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The livestock and plunder were theirs to keep. The Lord didn't begrudge them the resources they needed. Even in judgment, there is provision. He remains generous to His people, even in the hard passages.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: From the Arnon Valley to Mount Hermon—can you trace it on the map? The land was vast, stretching across the Jordan valley, from southern plains to northern heights. The Lord's promises stretch as wide as His hands can reach.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Hermon, Sirion, Senir—three names for one mountain, each from a different people. One place, known by many tongues. Sometimes the Lord speaks through the whole world around us, and all creation confesses His name.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: All the cities—the plain, Gilead, Bashan, all the way to Salecah and Edrei. When the Lord finishes a thing, He finishes it completely. Nothing is left half-done, no loose thread. His work endures.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Og's bedstead of iron—nine cubits long, four wide. His body was monstrous; his legend lived on in a bed on display in Rabbah. Even giants fade to relics. Their strength outlasts their lives, but not their purpose—they serve only as reminders that the Lord is greater still.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Moses began the distribution. From Aroer to half the Gilead highlands—Reuben and Gad received their portion, land east of the Jordan. The Lord cares not just about victory but about how His people are settled, provided for, and home.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The rest of Gilead and all Bashan went to half-Manasseh—the region of the Rephaim, the land of giants, now given to Jacob's grandchildren. The old order is passing away. The earth belongs to the Lord's people now.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Jair named the land after himself—Havvoth Jair, 'the settlements of Jair.' A man's name could outlive his body, written into the map itself. What do we want our lives to name? What mark do we hope to leave, not for ourselves, but for the generations after?
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Gilead to Machir. A few words, a whole inheritance. The Lord's provision is often given simply, without fanfare—a land, a name, a future, given as matter-of-factly as a parent gives a child the keys to the house.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Jabbok—where Jacob once wrestled the angel. Now it marks the border of Reuben and Gad's land, the boundary between their inheritance and the Ammonites'. The river was both gift and fence, a place of holy memory and a shield.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Arabah, the Jordan, the Salt Sea, the slopes of Pisgah—the land was mapped completely, borders clear, inheritance sure. Water and earth and stone all spoke the Lord's 'This is yours.' Geography becomes poetry when it carries the Lord's promise.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Before settling, they had to fight for their brothers' inheritance too. The command was clear: 'You shall pass over armed before your brothers.' Sometimes rest must wait, because love won't rest while others are still lacking. That's the shape of faithfulness.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The wives, children, and livestock would stay behind. Reuben and Gad had much livestock—and the Lord noticed, acknowledged what they possessed. His eye sees what we own, what we've been entrusted with, and He asks faithfulness with it first.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Until the Lord gives rest to your brothers, as He gave it to you. Then each would return to his own possession. Rest is earned together, not alone. Inheritance is fulfilled only when it's shared, when the whole people settles into the promise.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Joshua's commissioning began with his eyes. 'Your eyes have seen'—witness becomes foundation. He didn't need to guess or hope; he'd watched the Lord defeat two mighty kings. What we see of the Lord's faithfulness in our own lifetime becomes our reason to trust Him ahead.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Don't fear. The reason is simple: 'Yahweh your God Himself fights for you.' No appeal to courage, no rallying cry to bravery—only the assurance that the issue is already settled by Someone else's hand. That's the deepest peace there is.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Moses begged. After all the victories, after all the faithful leadership, he turned to prayer—not demands, not arguments, but simple asking. Even the greatest saints bring their deepest longings to the Lord as requests, not claims. Humility is the posture of the wise.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Moses' prayer opened with wonder. He marveled aloud: what god does works like this? His plea was rooted not in presumption but in awe at what the Lord had already shown. Sometimes we move the heart of God not by argument but by grateful amazement.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The good land, the fine mountain, Lebanon—Moses named what he longed for. He didn't hide his heart. But longing and receiving aren't always the same, and the Lord's 'no' can be as faithful as His 'yes.' Both are love.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Yahweh was angry—for your sakes. Even the refusal spoke of love. Moses couldn't enter because of Israel's sin at the waters, not his own. He bore the cost of the people's failure, a pattern that echoes forward to another who would bear far more.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: From Pisgah's top he would see it all—west, north, south, east. Mount Nebo, the view of the promised land from outside. A mercy and a heartbreak. The Lord gave him the sight of what he wouldn't possess, so that faith wouldn't die with his body.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Commission Joshua. Encourage him. Strengthen him. In his disappointment, Moses' task was to build up someone else's future. That's how we honor what God gives us—by passing the blessing onward with both hands open, holding nothing back.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Readers today hear an echo: we too wait in the valley before crossing over. The inheritance is promised, the Lord has shown His faithfulness, and yet the Jordan still flows between here and there. But Beth Peor—the house of Peor—was where the Lord made His covenant plain. We wait not in emptiness but in the house of His promise.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
